methods.label: Interior angles and shared sides
methods.explanation:
The congruent polygons have the same number of sides. Let each have \(n\) sides, and let the third polygon have \(k\) sides, where \(n,k\geq 3\) are integers. A regular \(n\)-gon has interior angle \(180^\circ-360^\circ/n\), so the angle condition gives
\[
2\left(180-\frac{360}{n}\right)+\left(180-\frac{360}{k}\right)=360.
\]
Simplifying and then factoring gives
\[
\frac{2}{n}+\frac{1}{k}=\frac12,
\qquad (n-4)(k-2)=8.
\]
Because \(1/k>0\), the first equation implies \(n>4\). Thus both factors in the second equation are positive integers. The positive divisors of \(8\) give exactly
\[
(n,k)=(5,10),\ (6,6),\ (8,4),\ (12,3).
\]
To find the outside perimeter, notice that the three angles fill the space around \(A\). Along each of the three rays separating neighboring polygons, two unit sides coincide. These three shared sides are internal, and each was counted twice in the sum of the individual perimeters. Hence
\[
P=2n+k-6.
\]
For the four possibilities above, the perimeters are respectively \(14,12,14,21\).

The last possibility is attainable: two regular dodecagons contribute angles of \(150^\circ\) each, and an equilateral triangle contributes \(60^\circ\). Place these angles consecutively around \(A\), matching their unit sides. Each convex polygon stays within its own angular region, so their interiors do not overlap. Therefore the largest possible perimeter is \(\boxed{21}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{D}}\).
